bridge: You have studied access checks, input interpretation and request handling. Use only the specified training application and fictional accounts.
teaching:
### Define the task before testing

Write the target, permitted operations, accounts, data and stopping conditions. Draw the main user journeys and identify which assets and permissions they involve.

Prioritise questions with meaningful consequences. Can a user read another user's record? Can supplied text become a database or shell instruction? Can one request perform an unintended second action?

### Keep each test tied to a rule

Record the expected behaviour, one controlled change and the actual result. Use the smallest permitted demonstration that establishes the issue. A tool's alert is a lead to investigate, not a finished finding.

### Explain the evidence

A report should identify the affected operation, prerequisites, repeatable lab steps and verified impact. Separate observed facts from possible wider consequences. Do not include unrelated credentials or other people's data.

### Verify the repair

Repeat the narrow failing case after the fix, then check the legitimate journey. Consider related entry points that share the same faulty logic. A fix that blocks the demonstration but breaks normal users or leaves another route open is incomplete.

Finish by recording coverage limits. An assessment has a scope and time window; it cannot promise that an application has no other vulnerabilities.
example:
Fictional note API packet
A owns n1; B owns n2; body max 100 chars.
Observed: A GET n2 ->200 with B's body.
Observed: PATCH n1 accepts owner=B from request body.
Observed: note preview inserts body using innerHTML despite plain-text contract.
Observed: A GET n1 ->200; B GET n2 ->200.
Scope: analyse packet only; make no external requests.
explanation: The first observation is object-authorisation failure, the second protected-property assignment, and the third a text/markup boundary problem. The packet supports design findings without requiring attack execution. Existing valid owner reads are essential regression cases.
exercise: Write three findings from the packet. Each needs problem, exact evidence, plausible impact, root cause, minimal repair and positive/negative verification cases. Include a scope and untested-behaviour section.
solution: Scope: analyse only the supplied fictional packet; no external requests were made. Untested: runtime exploitability, other endpoints, concurrency, deployment and real data. Finding 1 — cross-owner note disclosure. Evidence: A GET n2 returned 200 with B’s body although B owns n2. The intended rule is that each learner reads only their own notes. The supported impact is disclosure of that private note; the packet does not establish access to every note. Root cause: missing or ineffective object-owner enforcement on this read path. Repair: derive A from verified identity and constrain the object lookup/authorisation by owner. Recheck A/n1 and B/n2 succeed; A/n2 and B/n1 deny without bodies. Finding 2 — protected-field assignment. Evidence: PATCH n1 accepts owner=B from caller-controlled data. This can break the ownership policy; downstream effects need separate evidence. Root cause: a writable contract that includes or blindly copies a protected field. Repair: accept only the documented body field, derive owner from trusted state and reject unknown/protected keys. Recheck an ordinary permitted body update succeeds; supplied owner, wrong types and oversized bodies reject and leave ownership unchanged. Cover single and bulk update paths. Finding 3 — unsafe plain-text preview. Evidence: the preview uses innerHTML for a body whose contract is plain text. This establishes an unintended HTML-parsing boundary; it does not alone prove executable XSS under the deployed browser/policy. Repair: render body with textContent. Recheck ordinary text still displays and practice remains literal with no nested b element. Cover main, preview and export renderers rather than only one screen. A complete report keeps observed facts separate from predicted effects and records the regression result for each path.
challenge: Independently review a changed packet: ownership checks are fixed, but the export preview still uses innerHTML and bulk PATCH still accepts owner. State which original findings remain, identify the alternate paths and propose a regression matrix.
challenge_solution: The object-read finding can close only for verified paths. Rendering and protected-field issues remain in alternate paths. Include main/export views and single/bulk writes. A fix in the primary screen does not establish coverage of every entrypoint.
